DIVISION OF RETIREMENT BENEFITS IN DIVORCE AND QDROS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

PURPOSE AND IDENTIFICATION OF RETIREMENT INTEREST
This document addresses the division of a retirement plan interest between Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee, who married on June 14, 2015 and separated on March 2, 2026, arising from the dissolution of their marriage. It concerns the retirement plan or account known as Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan. It states legal background on how retirement benefits are treated in a dissolution and on the federal mechanism — a qualified domestic relations order, or QDRO — used to divide certain retirement plans. This document is not itself a qualified domestic relations order, is not a court order, and does not by itself direct any retirement plan or plan administrator to pay any amount to any person; it does not state whether Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee needs a QDRO or any other specific order for Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan, or how any specific benefit should be divided.

CALIFORNIA'S RULE: FULL COMMUNITY-PROPERTY SHARE OF RETIREMENT BENEFITS
Except in limited circumstances, a court is directed to make whatever orders are necessary or appropriate to ensure that each party receives that party's full community property share in any retirement plan, whether public or private, including all survivor and death benefits. The statute lists several non-exclusive mechanisms a court may use to accomplish this, including ordering the disposition of retirement benefits payable on death consistent with the equal-division statute, ordering a party to elect a survivor benefit annuity for the other party's benefit, and ordering a retirement plan to make payments directly to the nonmember party of that party's community property interest in the retirement benefits. Any division of a retirement plan interest of Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee under this document draws on this statutory framework.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the court shall make whatever orders are necessary or appropriate to ensure that each party receives the party's full community property share in any retirement plan, whether public or private, including all survivor and death benefits, including, but not limited to, any of the following: (1) Order the disposition of retirement benefits payable upon or after the death of either party in a manner consistent with Section 2550. (2) Order a party to elect a survivor benefit annuity or other similar election for the benefit of the other party, as specified by the court, when a retirement plan provides for that election, provided that no court shall order a retirement plan to provide increased benefits determined on the basis of actuarial value."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a) (California Legislative Information text), the court's authority and mechanisms for dividing retirement plan benefits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2610.)
  "Order a retirement plan to make payments directly to a nonmember party of the nonmember party's community property interest in retirement benefits."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), the direct-payment-to-nonmember-party mechanism (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2610.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one community-property jurisdiction directs courts to divide retirement benefits — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or retirement plan. Both citations in this clause come from the same statutory subdivision, Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a), and this clause, qdro_ca_public_plan_specific_statutes, and qdro_ca_retirement_division_limits all come from the same statutory section (§ 2610), so none of them is an independent source of authority from the others; they are presented together only because California is a single, real jurisdiction being used as an illustrative example. This clause does not state how a court values or apportions a benefit that was earned partly before marriage and partly during it (sometimes called a "time rule" or similar apportionment approach) — attempts to verify a citable primary source (statute or case) for that specific formula were not completed with confidence in the time available, so that topic is omitted here rather than described.

PUBLIC RETIREMENT SYSTEMS: A SEPARATE STATUTORY MECHANISM
California's general retirement-division statute expressly cross-references separate statutes that govern the division of specific public (governmental) retirement systems, rather than treating public-plan division as governed by the same mechanism as a private plan. It provides that, upon the agreement of the nonemployee spouse, a court may order division of accumulated community property contributions and service credit "as provided in the following or similar enactments," naming provisions of the Government Code and Education Code that govern named categories of state and local public retirement systems (including a state employees' retirement system, a state teachers' retirement system, county retirement systems, and a judges' retirement system). This confirms that a public, governmental retirement plan is not divided through the same federal mechanism described elsewhere in this document, but through a separate, system-specific statutory process.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Upon the agreement of the nonemployee spouse, order the division of accumulated community property contributions and service credit as provided in the following or similar enactments: (A) Article 2 (commencing with Section 21290) of Chapter 9 of Part 3 of Division 5 of Title 2 of the Government Code. (B) Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 22650) of Part 13 of Division 1 of Title 1 of the Education Code. (C) Article 8.4 (commencing with Section 31685) of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of Division 4 of Title 3 of the Government Code. (D) Article 2.5 (commencing with Section 75050) of Chapter 11 of Title 8 of the Government Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), the cross-reference to separate public-retirement-system division statutes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2610.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and confirms only what Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a)(3) itself says — that separate enactments exist and cross-references their Government Code and Education Code locations. It has not independently fetched or verified the text of those cross-referenced sections (e.g., Gov. Code § 21290 et seq. or Ed. Code § 22650 et seq.) or the operational procedures of any specific public system (such as CalPERS or CalSTRS) for processing a domestic relations order; this document does not describe those procedures because they were not independently verified against primary sources. This clause and qdro_ca_retirement_division_authority both derive from Cal. Fam. Code § 2610, so they are not independent of one another as sources.

LIMITS ON A COURT'S RETIREMENT-DIVISION ORDERS
A court's authority to divide retirement plan benefits is not unlimited. A court is not permitted to make an order that requires a retirement plan to make payments in a manner that increases the amount of benefits the plan provides, and, apart from the public-plan mechanism described elsewhere in this document, a court may not require a retirement plan to pay benefits to a party at any time before the member retires unless the plan itself provides for that.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A court shall not make an order that requires a retirement plan to do either of the following: (1) Make payments in a manner that will result in an increase in the amount of benefits provided by the plan. (2) Make the payment of benefits to a party at any time before the member retires, except as provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a), unless the plan so provides."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(b) (California Legislative Information text), limits on a court's retirement-division orders (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2610.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a court's retirement-division authority is bounded — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific plan. This clause and qdro_ca_retirement_division_authority both derive from Cal. Fam. Code § 2610 (the same statutory section, different subdivisions), so they are not independent of one another as sources.

FEDERAL LAW: THE ANTI-ASSIGNMENT RULE AND ITS QDRO EXCEPTION
Under federal law governing private-sector employee pension plans, each pension plan is required to provide that benefits under the plan may not be assigned or alienated. That general rule is subject to an exception: it does not apply to the creation, assignment, or recognition of a right to a benefit payable to a participant pursuant to a domestic relations order, where that order is determined to be a "qualified domestic relations order" (a QDRO). Where an order qualifies, each pension plan is required to pay benefits in accordance with the order's applicable requirements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Each pension plan shall provide that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), the general anti-assignment/anti-alienation rule for pension plans (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1056)
  "Paragraph (1) shall apply to the creation, assignment, or recognition of a right to any benefit payable with respect to a participant pursuant to a domestic relations order, except that paragraph (1) shall not apply if the order is determined to be a qualified domestic relations order. Each pension plan shall provide for the payment of benefits in accordance with the applicable requirements of any qualified domestic relations order."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(A) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), the qualified-domestic-relations-order exception to that rule (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1056)
  Known gap: This is a federal statute (ERISA), used as real evidence of the general rule and its domestic-relations-order exception for pension plans covered by this federal law. This clause combines two subparagraphs of the same statutory paragraph, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and § 1056(d)(3)(A), so they are not independent sources from one another, though both are independent of the California statutes cited elsewhere in this document (different sovereign, different statute). This clause does not address plans excluded from this federal scheme, which is addressed separately in this document.

WHAT A DOMESTIC RELATIONS ORDER MUST CONTAIN TO QUALIFY
Federal law defines a "qualified domestic relations order" as a domestic relations order that creates or recognizes an alternate payee's right to receive all or a portion of a participant's benefits under a plan, and that meets certain content requirements. To meet those content requirements, an order must clearly specify: the name and last known mailing address of the participant and of each alternate payee covered by the order; the amount or percentage of the participant's benefits to be paid to each alternate payee, or the manner in which that amount or percentage is to be determined; the number of payments or the period to which the order applies; and each plan to which the order applies. A domestic relations order that requires a plan to provide a type or form of benefit not otherwise available under the plan, or that requires increased benefits (measured by actuarial value), does not meet these requirements.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "the term "qualified domestic relations order" means a domestic relations order— (I) which creates or recognizes the existence of an alternate payee's right to, or assigns to an alternate payee the right to, receive all or a portion of the benefits payable with respect to a participant under a plan, and (II) with respect to which the requirements of subparagraphs (C) and (D) are met"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(B)(i) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), the definition of qualified domestic relations order (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1056)
  "A domestic relations order meets the requirements of this subparagraph only if such order clearly specifies— (i) the name and the last known mailing address (if any) of the participant and the name and mailing address of each alternate payee covered by the order, (ii) the amount or percentage of the participant's benefits to be paid by the plan to each such alternate payee, or the manner in which such amount or percentage is to be determined, (iii) the number of payments or period to which such order applies, and (iv) each plan to which such order applies."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(C) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), the required contents of a qualifying order (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1056)
  Known gap: This is a federal statute (ERISA), used as real evidence of the specific content requirements a domestic relations order must satisfy to be treated as a QDRO. This clause combines subparagraphs (B) and (C) of the same statutory paragraph, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3), so they are not independent sources from one another. This clause states the statutory definition and content requirements only; it does not state whether any particular order concerning any specific plan would qualify, which is a determination made by the plan administrator (addressed elsewhere in this document) and, ultimately, is fact- and plan-specific.

FEDERAL LAW DOES NOT REACH GOVERNMENTAL RETIREMENT PLANS
The federal statutory scheme described elsewhere in this document — including its anti-assignment rule and the qualified-domestic-relations-order exception to it — does not apply to a governmental plan. Federal law expressly excludes a governmental plan, along with certain other categories of plans, from the subchapter of federal law in which the QDRO mechanism appears. This is separate confirmation, from the federal side, of the same distinction reflected in California's cross-reference to separate public-retirement-system statutes: a public employer's retirement plan is not governed by the private-sector federal mechanism described in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The provisions of this subchapter shall not apply to any employee benefit plan if— (1) such plan is a governmental plan (as defined in section 1002(32) of this title)"
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1003(b)(1) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), the governmental-plan exclusion from ERISA's Title I subchapter (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1003)
  Known gap: This is a federal statute, used as real evidence that governmental plans are excluded from this part of ERISA — it is genuinely independent of the California statute cited elsewhere in this document (different sovereign, different law), even though both point toward the same real-world distinction. This clause does not itself define which retirement systems qualify as a "governmental plan" for this purpose (that definition appears in a separate cross-referenced section, 29 U.S.C. § 1002(32), which was not independently fetched and verified here) and does not state that any specific plan is or is not a governmental plan.

A QDRO IS A SEPARATE ORDER REQUIRING THE PLAN ADMINISTRATOR'S OWN DETERMINATION
Federal law does not treat a domestic relations order as automatically qualified once a court signs it. When a plan receives a domestic relations order, the plan administrator is required to promptly notify the participant and each alternate payee that the order was received and to describe the plan's procedures for determining whether the order is qualified, and, within a reasonable period after receipt, the plan administrator is required to determine whether the order is a qualified domestic relations order and to notify the participant and each alternate payee of that determination. This is a separate process, involving the plan administrator's own review, from the entry of a marital settlement agreement or dissolution judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "the plan administrator shall promptly notify the participant and each alternate payee of the receipt of such order and the plan's procedures for determining the qualified status of domestic relations orders, and (II) within a reasonable period after receipt of such order, the plan administrator shall determine whether such order is a qualified domestic relations order and notify the participant and each alternate payee of such determination."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(G)(i) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text), the plan administrator's notice and determination obligations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/1056)
  Known gap: This is a federal statute, used as real evidence that a domestic relations order goes through the plan administrator's own separate qualification process. It does not state how long that process typically takes in practice, what any specific plan's internal procedures require, or whether any specific order will be found qualified — those are plan-specific and fact-specific questions this clause does not address.

Retirement plan or account name: Acme, Inc. 401(k) Plan

☐ Public/governmental plan (subject to a separate, system-specific division statute rather than a federal QDRO)
☐ Private-sector plan (potentially subject to a qualified domestic relations order under federal law)
